extracted.intended_audience: educated Protestant readers, theologians, and clergy debating church authority and sacramental theology
extracted.subtask_description: A polemical, scripturally-grounded critique of Roman Catholic claims about the present Kingdom of God, papal authority, sacramental rites (consecration, baptism, Eucharist), immortality of the soul, purgatory, and eternal punishment. The page explains correct interpretive/ceremonial standards and rejects various abuses as non-scriptural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of the Kingdom of God
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kingdome of God is not yet come; the present Church is not (yet) Christ's Kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues from Scripture (e.g., Acts 1, Mark 9) that Christ's Kingdom begins at the day of Judgment and that promises about 'the Kingdom' refer to a future, not present, consummation. Uses scriptural context (e.g. Transfiguration, Ascension, Pentecost) to show phrases like 'some shall not taste death' are not proof that the Kingdom began at the Resurrection.

rubrics_metrics.name: No single man or assembly is Christ's earthly mouth
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought not to be 'some one Man, or Assembly, by whose mouth our Saviour (now in heaven) speaketh' to represent Christ universally to all Christians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects the doctrine that any pope or particular assembly speaks for Christ; warns that claiming such power leads to conflicts with civil sovereigns and creates confusion among subjects about lawful obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Pope is not Vicar General of Christ
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that the Pope is the Vicar Generall of Christ in the present Church is false and leads to political and spiritual abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contends that papal claims (e.g., requiring kings to be crowned by bishops, oaths of obedience by bishops to the Pope, canons asserting subjects absolved from obedience) are non-scriptural. Illustrates social/political harms when papal and civil aims conflict, producing 'Darknesse in mens understanding.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Coronation by a bishop is not the source of regal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary for a Christian King to receive his crown by a Bishop in order to derive 'Dei Gratia' or legitimate authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against the doctrine that episcopal coronation is the moment a king receives God's favour; historical and scriptural counterexamples are cited to show kingship is not contingent on pontifical ceremony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clergy/laity distinction and tithe claims are abusive
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating pastors and other ministers as a separate 'Clergy' with divine right to revenue (tithes) as the Levites had is a mistaken transfer from Israel to Christendom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains historical origin of the term 'clergy' and criticizes the imposition of tithes and ecclesiastical revenues as a double tribute (state + clergy). Compares ancient Israel's context to expose inappropriateness of claiming Jure Divino tribute by ecclesiastics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecration means dedication, not change of nature
rubrics_metrics.description: To Consecrate is to offer, give, or dedicate an object or person to God by separating it from common use; it does not change the nature or substance of the thing consecrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes consecration (sanctifying use) from 'Conjuration' or 'Incantation' which would claim an actual change of nature. Uses examples (bread and wine) to reject literal transubstantiation and labels claims of nature-changing consecrations as superstitious or incantatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transubstantiation is a conjuration/abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: The priest's words 'This is my Body' are equivalent to 'This signifies, or represents my Body' and taken literally they are an abuse; transubstantiation (real change of bread into Christ's body) is not scriptural or ancient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that claims that any priest's consecration instantly changes any bread's substance were only formalized later (alleged around Innocent III) and are akin to Egyptian conjurers: a delusion of the senses and a form of idolatry when worship is required of the bread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual words and gestures must be decent and significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceremonies, words, and gestures in consecrations and sacraments ought to be decent, significant, and conformable to the nature of the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses biblical examples (Moses consecrating Tabernacle and Aaron; Solomon's dedication of the Temple) to show that proper consecration involved simple, rational prayer, anointing, washing—no exorcised water, no impertinent added words or charmed gestures. Criticizes additions like spittle, repeated exorcisms, and theatrical processions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exorcisms and incantations in sacraments are improper
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent exorcisms, conjurations, and charms used in Baptism, Eucharist, and other rites turn consecration into incantation and are unscriptural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists examples: making 'holy water' with conjurations, benediction of salt as 'Conjured Salt', the priest blowing thrice on a child's face and reciting exorcisms at the church door, benediction of oil as driving away 'the Host of the Devill.' These practices are condemned as not found in apostolic precedent and as superstitious.

rubrics_metrics.name: The rites of the early Church lacked exorcisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Consecrations and baptisms in Scripture and apostolic practice did not employ exorcised water or incantatory rites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts that John, Philip, Moses, and early pastors performed baptisms and consecrations with simple washing, anointing, prayers and offerings—no exorcised liquids, no spittle rites—so later additions cannot be justified by apostolic authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immortality of the soul is not proven as natural by Scripture
rubrics_metrics.description: The immortality of the soul (souls living separated from the body) is not shown by Scripture to be natural to human nature, but must be understood as a gift of God's special grace for the elect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Ecclesiastes and Job to argue that 'soul' in Scripture often means 'life' or 'living creature' and that passages suggesting immortality are better read as promises of resurrection for the elect, not as proof of inherent, natural immortality of all souls (including the wicked).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eternal torments and 'everlasting death' need different interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'Everlasting fire' or 'Everlasting torments' do not necessarily prove individual, unending conscious torment; they can mean punishment continuing as long as the kind of mankind endures (i.e., perpetuated by successive sinners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposes that the fire or torments prepared for the wicked may continue forever in succession, though not implying that any one person will be tormented eternally; thus 'everlasting' can describe the perpetuity of punishment as a phenomenon rather than the unending conscious duration for each individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purgatory is founded on a false assumption of natural soul-survival
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of Purgatory arises from assuming natural immortality of separated souls; if immortality is granted by grace only, then Purgatory is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that if souls do not naturally persist until resurrection, the concept of an intermediate, purgatorial state for cleansing is an innovation built on disputable premises and earlier pagan/Greek notions of the soul rather than apostolic teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural interpretation must consider whole scope/context
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscure or ambiguous New Testament passages should be read in the context of the whole Scripture to avoid erroneous doctrines (e.g., present Kingdom, natural immortality, purgatory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses examples (Mark 9:1, Acts 1:6, references to Abraham being 'living') to show that literal or isolated readings produce false inferences; recommends grammatical, contextual, and whole-Scripture comparison (e.g., Luke, Matthew, Thessalonians) to determine true meaning.
